And at the bottom of page 21, the last two lines in B/C/S and on to the next page -- well, the last two lines my English translation says: "These are all regular things we need to carry out every day with all these forces, prepare ourselves as if the war will happen tomorrow." And as a matter of fact, that's what the VJ did, didn't it, you were making extensive preparations for a war in the spring, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's go to page 22, the second paragraph. This is still General Bojovic speaking. And he said: "We should strengthen our special forces in that field, in particular in Kosovo and Metohija, along the rim too," I'll skip a little bit. It says: "That means police forces, reconnaissance, anti-sabotage units, and so on. We should have all these forces -- we should have these forces in all our garrisons in Kosovo and Metohija and we should be prepared if the orders come and we can expect such orders to come, to participate in combat with the MUP but in a specific way, so as not to damage policy, the state, in other words not to use tanks and artillery." Now, a few questions follow from that. In late January and early February the VJ and 3rd Army and the Pristina Corps were making preparations for the expected possible war that was going to come with the KLA and/or NATO in the spring, were you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina Corps as part of the 3rd Army was engaged in January and February in preparing a special-purpose plan, that is, defending the country from multi-national forces, from -- coming from Macedonia and Albania, and armed insurgency. That is my answer to your question what specifically the Pristina Corps was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Grom 3 had been prepared in January of 1999, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the level, I cannot remember when it was prepared on each level. But Grom 3 is this particular plan from the General Staff level down to different tactical levels below, but I believe it was prepared by end January/February.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on the 16th of February, I think it's Exhibit P2808, your Pristina Corps number 455-1 was your directive, your plan in preparation for those possible events in the spring, correct? You'll see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to be a little more precise. This is not a directive, because that's not what the corps command does; it is a whole plan. We see the order of the Pristina Corps command to crush and destroy Siptar terrorist forces in specified locations, without specifying the time when the plan would be activated. The plan was to be activated upon receipt of a special signal and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I misspoke in referring to that as a directive. I would like to return to 939 for a couple more items. And, General, I want to look at page 24 in the B/C/S. And it's page 26 of the English. I'll tell you this is General Dimitrijevic speaking, and I want to link this back to what Bojovic had said before too. And it relates to the issue of using the artillery and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I need page 26 of the English and 24 of the B/C/S and the top of the page for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic is saying in paragraph 3 on the English and the first paragraph on the top of page 24 for you, General: "You know that when on 15 October President Milosevic signed, or rather, made the agreement with Holbrooke, that those forces were not destroyed as had been said but dispersed, but the fact is that none were concentrated in this area. Since then they have been coming back, organizing, arming themselves, and all the rest. Why has this not been done before, and I think that in the existing international conditions this is the primary task of the MUP, they should carry out anti-terrorist operations, not frontal operations where they first have artillery preparation and then capture or destroy whatever they find afterwards." And the next paragraph: "So as far as the army is concerned, I think that in this phase, in addition to all these preparations, activities should be focused on protecting the border, while as far as the MUP is concerned, let me stress this once again, on the anti-terrorist operations, to be carried out primarily against commands, staffs, and we know where they are." Now, General, isn't it true that international community's complaints about the activities of the security forces, the army and the MUP, in their actions in Kosovo in 1998 focus largely on what they term disproportionate force in those anti-terrorist operations? That's what General Bojovic and General Dimitrijevic are talking about here, isn't it, that artillery preparation, the use of heavy weapons in those kinds of actions, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal knowledge from 1998 and early 1999 is this: Only on one occasion at official meetings between the OSCE mission and the liaison team with OSCE was it stated that there was disproportionate use of force on the 8th of January against Slapuzane village where a tank projectile was fired. Nowhere else in the documents that I was able to see regarding cooperation with the OSCE mission or in any reports from my superiors or underlings did I find this complaint, that in 1998 the forces of the corps used force disproportionately. And what Mr. -- What General Dimitrijevic is saying, he's talking about artillery preparation theatrically as a possibility. I'm not aware of a single action of the army when they were supporting the MUP and providing artillery preparation prior to the action. I understand that General Dimitrijevic is saying that should not be done, that should not be done. He's not saying it was done, it had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You told us just now according to your personal knowledge you only knew of one occasion. You weren't aware that there were widespread allegations that this kind of use of heavy weapons was being taken against civilians in those operations against the terrorists in Kosovo in 1998? You didn't read about it? You didn't hear about it on TV or the radio or the newspapers? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to speak in concrete terms. I tried to refer to the documentation of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army dealing with our cooperation with the OSCE mission. I tried to invoke my contacts with my subordinate officers in 1998, my contacts with my superiors in 1999, and to say that I have no information corroborating these allegations. As far as media are concerned, I remember one occurrence in particular from the second half of 1998 when the location of Obrinje was mentioned in this context, wherein the commander of the corps and the whole corps command ordered a detailed gathering of information to investigate whether the army had been involved. That is what I personally know from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to the next paragraph. This is still General Dimitrijevic, bottom of 26 and top of 27 in the English. He says: "I do not think we could work in any other weighty moment anyway, and as far as General Marjanovic's dilemma is concerned, I also have to say the same. I don't know what is being presented there and whether what is being presented by the Joint Command is this or something else entirely. I was personally present when the minister here was received by the chief, the minister of the interior, and when the man unambiguously stated that the backbone of terrorism was broken, that terrorism was destroyed, and that this was a showdown with the remains of the terrorist gangs, criminals." Now, we see here General Dimitrijevic is making reference to the Joint Command, and as I understand this - and we've seen this topic before - that there's -- the army has a view that the police and perhaps the politicians as well are presenting a false picture, a too rosy picture, if you will, about the status of the terrorists in Kosovo. Is that consistent with what you saw and knew about in January of 1999, that is, that things in Kosovo were worse than were being portrayed in public by the minister of interior, the police, the politicians?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to see where the Prosecutor read the word "politicians."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I didn't. That's not anything Mr. Dimitrijevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, well. Well, then tell that to the witness instead of asking him whether the politicians conveyed a message or not. And as long as I'm on my feet, I would like to say that this text had better be read by General Lazarevic than having the English translation read, whereas we get the translation back into Serbian. We're just wasting time that way. If Mr. Hannis wants something read, then he should have General Lazarevic read it in the original Serbian. That's at least my suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. That will depend on the circumstances. Mr. Hannis, the question becomes very complicated when you throw in the last line, that's line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, based on -- let me withdraw that question and try to ask a different one. Based on your knowledge and experience of what the situation in Kosovo was with regard to the extent of the problem of terrorism, are you aware of any public statements that were being made that presented a too rosy picture, a false picture, suggesting that it was much better than you knew it to be?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall reading at that time any public comments about the overall situation of security, but at that time in early 1999, as Chief of Staff and later commander, it was my belief that the situation was very, very unfavourable because on the 8th of January, 1999, in the middle of this peace and international presence, eight soldiers were kidnapped by terrorists, which constituted a dramatic deterioration of the overall state of affairs in Kosovo and Metohija. This is just an example, because in your previous question you seem to ask me what my view was of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you agree with the statement that the backbone of terrorism was broken, that terrorism was destroyed in January of 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal knowledge is that towards the end of summer 1998, or rather, in end September to be more precise, the backbone of terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was indeed neutralised. But as far as the month of January is concerned, they had rebuilt and restored in many ways [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness said, 52, 25, the witness said: Additionally strengthened, that the backbone of terrorism was rebuilt, restored, and additionally strengthened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, in connection with that last reference to an opinion expressed by the minister of the interior, I want to segue into your dealings with the MUP. As part of your business, you regularly received information or intelligence from the MUP, did you not?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the honourable Prosecutor means me personally, whether somebody from the MUP gave it to me as the commander, but the corps command and primarily the security department, primarily through the sector of state security, exchanged information, that much is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was your security officer when you were head of the Pristina Corps, when you were commander of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the security department of the corps command was Colonel Momir Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: He had also been -- well, how long had he been in that position? He was also in that position in 1998 as well, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I found him there as Chief of Staff when I arrived in the corps, but I don't know how long he had been there before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in your dealings with him, how would you describe his abilities and his work as head of the security department for the Pristina Corps? Was he knowledgeable?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Stojanovic, to the best of my recollection, was born in Djakovica. He was familiar with the general situation in terms of security, interethnic, international security situation. And at that time, I felt that, being familiar with the situation, he was successfully carrying out his duties in compliance with his authority and powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to show you Exhibit P2945, and this may take a minute to come up. General, this is a newspaper article dated the 22nd of November, 2002 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Bakrac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood that newspaper articles cannot be exhibits, especially when they deal with something somebody else stated they cannot be put to this witness. All the more so as General Momir Stojanovic will be coming to testify here very soon. That's my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've just shot the objection down, Mr. Bakrac, by telling me that he's coming to give evidence, because obviously Mr. Hannis ought to prepare the way for anything he's going to ask him when he does arrive; and therefore, it is appropriate in this instance to use something he's reported to have said to a newspaper. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, you see the first page of that article. That is General Stojanovic that you're talking about, right?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's General Stojanovic. He's a colonel in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if you could go to page 2 of the B/C/S in this article, there is a document that purports to be from the colonel at the time, directed to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Do you see that, that's item number 2 on that page, and it's from the Pristina Corps command security sector. It's signed by him and has a stamp, and it's dated the 11th of November, 1998. I know you weren't the commander of the Pristina Corps at that time, but were you aware that the head of security for the Pristina Corps was providing information to the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija in November of 1998?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I never saw this. It's the first time I've seen it now on the screen. I assume that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct. And before today, you were not aware that Colonel, now General, Stojanovic had given such an interview and talked about those things in the paper in 2002 or 2000, I'm not sure? It looks like 2000 on my copy.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that he gave an interview or talked to a journalist. I'm not sure whether he was in the security service at the time or not. I recall that, but I didn't really read the papers and I saw this among the exhibits of the Prosecution. But I really hadn't seen this document before. I don't know if it's from a newspaper or if it's scanned from some document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, is Politika not a newspaper you would read?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is not Politika, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is the Nedeljni Telegraf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that a newspaper you would not read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did read whatever I could lay my hands on occasionally, but it's not a newspaper that anyone is bound to read, either in the army or myself. I remember that allegedly he gave an interview at the time, if that's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was it you retired from active army service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 5th of October, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So whenever this interview was given, it was given at a time when he was one of your subordinate officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, that's not how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I misunderstand the situation then, Mr. Hannis, I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, when did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, is this the Telegraph from England, the local one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I'll follow-up a couple questions on what Judge Bonomy asked, but let's turn to the next page of the B/C/S. And although you may not have read this newspaper, it appears that you did talk to them because that's your picture and that purports to be an interview with you by this very same newspaper. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked me two questions, that I spoke to someone, I don't understand who I spoke to - does this relate to Colonel Stojanovic; and secondly, as far as I can see, this is not an interview; and lastly, I spoke to a journalist, Antic, who originated from Kosovo, on one occasion about what was going on in Kosovo. And I recognise part of that conversation in this text, but it was not an actual interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who was this journalist Antic that you spoke to and can you give us some details about the circumstances of that, when and where and what was it about?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four question, if I can answer them all, I'll do my best but I ask for assistance. I know of the last name Antic, I don't know the first name. When and where I spoke to him I really can't recall, I can't be precise. It might have been in Nis on some occasion, but it was not about a specific topic. He did not put questions to me. I simply generally spoke about what was going on in Kosovo and Metohija, why this had happened after the Kumanova Agreement, and that was the topic of our conversation as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you read out the headline in bold letter next to your picture, can you read us what that says starting with "Mnoge."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Many actions of the MUP of Serbia were leaked, because in their intelligence service they had Siptars who later became terrorist commanders."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And during 1998 and 1999, were you aware of this problem with the MUP having a lot of leaks or their -- many of their actions being leaked?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say that, when the author of this article writes that, it refers primarily to intelligence information of the State Security Service within the Ministry of the Interior. I was aware of the problem that to a certain extent, sometimes a large extent, there was misinformation and we had losses, because we engaged the organs of state security and organs securing the state border in the wrong places, and that was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that is something you talk about in what's written here, that sometimes you were provided -- "you," meaning the army, were provided information by the MUP about where groups might be trying to cross the border with weapons and you would go there and no one would show up or nothing would happen, right? Is that the kind of thing that was happening in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly -- well, I believe the Prosecutor when he says that's what it says here. I really don't see what the text says, but the gist of my assessment and the gist of what I said refers to the following: Intelligence information which we received was not always relevant, it was not always precise, and this led to losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, so I take it from your earlier answers that you had not seen this text before just now when I showed it to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the list of documents, I saw that an interview of mine was to be presented, but I didn't deal with that. I expected it to be presented here and I thought I would have an opportunity to clarify it. But I don't see this actually because the writing is very small on the screen, so I can't read what this journalist wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what I would propose to do, General, is that I can give you a copy and perhaps during the break you can read it and after the break bring it to our attention. If there's anything in here that you find is incorrect or needs clarification, we'll talk about it after the break. Is that satisfactory? But I do want to ask you about the last paragraph, and I can hand you my hard copy right now. It's the very last paragraph on the right-hand column, it's under the area that I blocked out in pink, it's the very last few lines. And you want to read that one for us? It starts out with: "Maybe I shouldn't ..."

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "'Maybe I shouldn't say this, but it must be said that the MUP of Serbia and its political mentors were -- cost us,' concluded General Lazarevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I don't know, there seem to be some difficulty. Is "political mentors cost us"? I have a draft translation that says"destroyed us." Could you read that line again.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure, it's short. Please.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "'Maybe I shouldn't say this, but for the sake of the truth I must say that the MUP of the Serbia and its political mentors destroyed us in Kosovo and Metohija.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is that correct? Is that how you felt about things? In 2000 when you talked about this?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have to say, although there is a dash here, it looks like quotation marks. That's how I ended the conversation with the journalist. And if I may be allowed to read the context and see what all this is about, I might be able to add something. But this term "political mentors," I don't really understand it, to tell you the truth, and I cannot confirm that these are my words, not my original words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, if you were trying to tell us who the political mentors of the MUP of Serbia were in 1998 and 1999, who would you be thinking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has already answered this question, that he doesn't recall having said that in that context and that he doesn't understand what the word "mentor" means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think he said he doesn't remember saying what's here. He says he can't confirm -- in English he can't confirm that these are his words. But he has said, Mr. Hannis, that he doesn't understand the term "political mentors."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do you understand what the term "mentor" means?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mentor" is a term, as far as I know, used in developing a topic. It's the leader who assists someone to carry out a task, directs him, monitors, gives suggestions, and it's used primarily in academic work, a mentor or a leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Who in 1998 or 1999 would have been a leader or one who gave suggestions to the MUP in carrying out tasks? Who in the political field would that describe, if anybody, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now we have a double translation. Mr. Lazarevic mentioned "voditelj" and now he got back "vodja," which is really leader and what we have in English and "voditelj" doesn't mean leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how would you translate "voditelj," Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Lazarevic used term "mentor," definitely it's not leader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it was translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Or somebody who guides somebody else, actually, is -- or advise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the question you want to ask, Mr. Hannis, is who from the political sphere might have fitted that bill in relation to the MUP in 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, General? That's the question I would ask.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard the question and to the best of my knowledge, for the organization and execution of all the tasks of the organs and units of the MUP, it was the minister of the interior of Serbia who was in charge. And who he reported to in the hierarchy I really don't know, I can only assume, but this is what I read in the official document, the Law on Internal Affairs, and that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, if we were to break now the witness would have a chance to read the document and we could resume at quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you have a chance to review Exhibit P2945 and the portion of the interview that referred to you or the article that referred to you?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is there -- well, what comment would you like to make to us about that? Does it refresh your recollection? Is it accurate in terms of what you said as far as you can tell or what?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the leave of the Trial Chamber, I would like to make one comment. I would like to point out certain passages in this text and the very way the topic is dealt with, which goes to show that these are not my words, that they are outside the context of this brief conversation we had. And if the Trial Chamber allows me, I would take it point by point. I need just a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it really is a matter for you at the moment. Nothing's been confirmed as accurate, so how do you want to proceed with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think I want to allow him the opportunity, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- to hear specifically what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lazarevic, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reading this text in the short time I had, I noticed first that it is not in the format of an interview, that is, a question-and-answer session -- at least that's my understanding of an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- And in that sense, I could question the authenticity of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter whether it's an interview or not. The real question is whether it's an accurate reflection of what you said or thought, and if you could concentrate on that, that would help us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's understood, Your Honour. Let me point out that there is no date here, so it didn't help me remember exactly when this happened, the journalist, the reporter, it doesn't mention it. And moving on, towards the end of the introduction, this passage in bold print, he says to his readers: "A commander of the 3rd Army and Chief of Staff of many years." I don't understand what the author of the text is trying to tell his readership, Chief of Staff of what of many years? I really don't know what he means. And towards the end of the first column on the left-hand side, the last few short sentences could certainly not have been uttered by me - and I'll explain that. The reporter says: "Each documented proposal of ours was met by the then-leadership with the words: 'You are too radical.'" I was never in a position to warn the state leadership about anything, nor did I discuss it with anyone. And if you allow me to point out, the interview with Colonel Stojanovic contains the very same words, the third column -- the middle of the third column. And I particularly want to emphasise the second column of this alleged interview with me. "The obstruction of our proposals had gone so far that for years they failed to expand the border belt from 100 metres to 5 kilometres," something that first General Pavkovic insisted on and then later I. This is complete nonsense because at this point I had been in Kosovo and Metohija for a year. It can't be true that I was trying to mislead both the readership or this reporter. He knows exactly when I had come to Kosovo and he knows exactly what I was proposing and how I was supporting General Pavkovic first and then the leadership. Then the fourth column, the last passage: "We warned more than once that customs authorities and services are seriously corrupted." I didn't know any customs officers or authorities in Kosovo and I couldn't have said anything of the kind. And finally, concerning the last paragraph, we discussed it at the previous session, about mentors, that's the term used here. If you allow me, I want to point out something on the next page, that same word is used by the author to explain the position of Zoran Mijatovic in this frame: "You and your mentor Stojiljkovic." All this leads me to conclude, as I did before, that I never used that term myself. And I want to say in conclusion, if this author had a general conversation with me about the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, he abused it to turn it into a completely different story of his own. I do accept that I met with this journalist, we discussed this general topic, but I certainly didn't say some of these things written here. Those are simply not my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, General, let me see if I can pick out a few then that you would agree are your statements or were your statements. First of all, when did you become commander of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: January -- maybe not January, March or April 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if this article is written in November of 2000 and you became 3rd Army commander sometime between January and April, we can narrow down the time-frame of your meeting or conversation with the journalist to sometime between those dates, right, sometime in 2000?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I really cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall telling the journalist that all those who would have had a decisive role, those who made the highest decisions, they now want to blame the army and the Pristina Corps? That's how you felt in 2000, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not so. That's not so, because I approached that conversation and that topic from the viewpoint of inconsistency of certain information, security-related information at the time in 1998 and early 1999. That was the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The article attributes to you this, that: "The federal government decided to expand the bordering area to 5 kilometres only in the summer of 1998, when Siptar terrorists already occupied half the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and when our bordering units were cut off." You said that, didn't you? You've told us something similar here.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that this position was the result of our previous position, when for years we had been warning -- sorry, from that previous passage where the author says I -- quotes me as saying that I had been warning for years; I had not been there for years. That the border belt should be expanded, that was my position, and in the month of March, when I was meeting Mr. Lilic at the border and I believe he was accompanied by General Perisic, I told them both that that should be done as soon as possible. But I don't recall discussing this with this journalist in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you discuss it in that way with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did, within the circle of people who toured units from the superior command or with people who inspected the state border, such as the state officials, including Mr. Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next sentence says: "'During all that time,' General Lazarevic continues, 'there were accusations going around that the army was guilty of Siptar terrorists having armed themselves.'" Is that something you said?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said, not even in other conversations, that at that time in 1998 somebody was blaming the army for the fact that there were too many weapons in Kosovo and Metohija. But it was primarily the task of the army to prevent the smuggling of weapons, but this whole further story that somebody was blaming the army or the customs authorities, all that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Two questions about it. You're saying it's not true that you said that, right, that's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say it to this journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying the fact is not true as well? Are you saying that there were no accusations going around that the army was guilty of terrorists having armed themselves? If you know.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot deny that there were maybe some people who blamed the army as well for the fact that terrorists were being supplied with weapons from Albania, but it is a fact that the army was dealing with its mission to prevent it with all available resources. I just want to point out that these arms shipments took place even before 1998, in 1997, for instance, when I wasn't even there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And lastly, with regard to the last paragraph, are you saying now that you didn't mention anything about the political mentors of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I really don't remember a single occasion or a single person to whom I would have spoken using the term "political mentor." But this same author uses the same term with another alleged interviewee, whom I didn't even know. It could be this Mijatovic man who already testified here, the one from MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then should the last paragraph read that it was the MUP of Serbia that destroyed you in Kosovo and only the MUP?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, really, I'm afraid I'm being asked to suppose what the author should have written. At that time I had my own position and I still have my own position, which is different to what this writer wrote, and he may have known the situation in Kosovo even better than I did. And I think he used the meeting or a conversation he had with me to tell a story of his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you just said: "At that time I had my own position and I still have my own position ..." What was your position?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my position specifically is that I, as an officer, am not blaming heaven knows which agencies in the state. I as the Chief of Staff was in charge of securing the state border, and I walked most of that border personally. And I noticed during those tours of inspection that the protection and defence of the state border had not been organized in the best possible way; that was the main observation I made. As Chief of Staff of the corps, I suggested measures to the corps commander, I suggested measures to the Chief of General Staff, and then in November he rejected them after once accepting them at the collegium meeting. In November when he came to Djakovica to visit, he changed his view and rejected my proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's not clear to me from that answer. Is your position then that no politicians and nobody from MUP has any blame for what happened in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that I neither knew the politicians who were in charge of security issues at state level or in that area, such as head of state, the Assembly, et cetera, nor did I know anyone from the leadership of the MUP or the police at that time. I'm saying specifically as Chief of Staff of the corps, I walked dozens of kilometres of the state border. I wrote reports and briefed all the way up to the Chief of General Staff that the security is not the best. And I made -- developed special studies at army level for that border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't want to interrupt. 68, lines 20 to 23. It's completely different what the witness has said. He said that in November when the Chief of the General Staff came, he accepted my proposal, although he previously rejected it. So previously to November it was rejected one time, and then the Chief of the General Staff came to visit and then accepted the proposal by General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That needs to be clarified, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's the opposite way at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, did you hear the comments of Mr. Zecevic just now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I want to recall that we had a witness here who was a member of the General Staff at the time, Colonel Cucak, who confirmed the same thing. Second, documents were introduced from the collegium meetings of the Chief of General Staff, I believe these are Prosecution exhibits, and the collegium, including General Perisic, did not accept proposals at the corps command and the 3rd Army command dealing with complex security for the state border. And third, General Perisic arrived in early November 1998 to the forward command post of the corps in Djakovica, I briefed him. And based on that briefing and report I made and his own personal tours of some units, he changed his personal position and he ordered additional security to be provided for the state border and also that a study be made at the level of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, I want to go back to page 68, line 24. I'm not sure you completely answered my question about whether your position was that no politicians and nobody from MUP has any blame for what happened. You said: "What I'm trying to say is that I neither knew the politicians who were in charge of security issues at the state level or in that area." Now, we know in 1998 that you knew certain state officials by virtue of the fact that you met with them at Joint Command meetings, one meeting in August and four meetings in September 1998, that included Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Minic. And you've also told us I think about Mr. Lilic coming on tour with the Chief of Staff. So you did know those politicians, correct? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know those people who held that positions, but I didn't know their responsibilities for securing the state border. That's what I meant when I said I didn't know who had functional responsibility for the state border. I thought it was the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, as far as I know. I didn't know those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, I think you're making it too narrow for one thing. We were talking about your statement in this newspaper article, at least what's attributed to you, about saying that: "Maybe I shouldn't say this, but for the sake of the truth it's necessary to say that the MUP of Serbia destroyed us in Kosovo and Metohija." I would suggest that's not just limited to problems with security of the state border, but it's broader than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, my learned friend Mr. Hannis went through this text in detail, and the answer he received was that these words were not uttered by Mr. Lazarevic to the journalist. And now he goes back to the question what this sentence means. I believe it is superfluous and unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I understood he took particular issue with the reference to political mentors. And then I asked him a follow-up question about: "Is it your position then that neither the MUP nor politicians had any blame for the problems in Kosovo?" And I got an answer that he didn't know any of the politicians and there was nothing discussed about MUP. I'm trying to follow-up on that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, he has already said page 68, I think, line 2 that these are not his -- this is not what he said. Now, your question is based on what's attributed to him, and the objection is that that's already been dealt with. So you need to approach it in a different way rather than harking back to something that's not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I hear what you're saying, Your Honour. I didn't read his answer to be a non-acceptance of that beyond political mentor, but I will take your point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps -- do I read too much into it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, maybe not when he says: "This is different to what the writer wrote -- my position is different to what the writer wrote."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you should reformulate the question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, you said you have your position -- you had your position and you have your position. Isn't it your position that someone other than the army was to blame for what happened in Kosovo? You don't think it was the army's fault, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was a whole series of questions regarding the security of the state border and the supplying of terrorists with weapons. And now we hear a new question: Who is to blame for the general picture and the general, the overall, situation in Kosovo? Why doesn't our colleague Mr. Hannis say exactly what he means?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, because I'm starting from a reference that said: Somebody destroyed us in Kosovo. I'm trying to find out who he's blaming for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, we repel that objection. Please proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, do I need to repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you need not. I want to say emphatically that these last two sentences are not mine, they're not my words. The political mentors of the MUP of Serbia who are responsible for what happened in Kosovo, are something I did not discuss, I did not mention to this reporter or any other reporter. As for the second part of the question that the honourable Prosecutor has repeated a number of times, I tried to explain from my personal experience, my personal viewpoint, and in view of what I personally tried to do as an officer in charge of the border, what our problems were but from the standpoint of the army. Of course I pointed out to problems with coordination and accessibility of information. We mentioned that before, but that was in another context.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. I think you've gone beyond answering my question. Let me move on to another topic. I want to ask you: Did you have a chance to review the DVDs of your interview this weekend? I think you told us that at the beginning, but I wanted to confirm.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I was focusing on the part of the interview that I particularly objected to, and I said that this interview with me was misrepresented to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you're talking about in particular the question of how many meetings of the Joint Command you attended. Is that what you're referring to now?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because last Friday it was suggested that I had not confirmed my attendance at any of the meetings and video-clip of 12 minutes was shown. I asked the Trial Chamber to allow me to check whether my memory's correct, that there is another passage in that interview when the military analyst asked me whether I attended or not, and I answered that I do not deny having personally attended at one of those meetings. And I found that passage over the weekend on a videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I can read from that one or we can play it - do you have a preference? - that portion of the interview that talks about attending another meeting.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My suggestion is that I read the information from the DVD relating to those two minutes of my reply, and then if that can be shown in the courtroom I would like to ask it to be shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. Over the weekend I also viewed the DVD. And I think what General Lazarevic is referring to is tape V0005252-1-A from 57 to 59 is the minutes, so it's up to Your Honour as to whether it should be read out or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think at this minute preparations are being made to play it. Is that right, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And if the general and I are on the same page - no pun intended - I think we're starting at page 94, yes, page 94 of the English. And as background, Mr. Coo has asked the question about the General's awareness of the existence of the Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, tell us if this is not the right starting point.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it does refer to this, but here's the video and we'll hear that.

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Mr. Lazarevic: [Interpretation] And I did know that they had meetings in Pristina" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we need to back up a little bit. The end of Mr. Coo's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "Mr. Lazarevic: [Interpretation] And that is not what I have been saying. I agree with what you said toward the end, that this body was primarily there for the coordination of political, diplomatic, and other activities, and that they naturally had a great deal of intelligence from MUP and the VJ and the state security about the situation in the province. And I did know that they had meetings in Pristina, which were also attended by the army commander. I also said that I was there with the corps commander and that we were -- had a meeting at a civilian building and where information was exchanged. If I reviewed all the combat documents, maybe I would find out that I perhaps attended towards the end of the year one more of these informative meetings, but I cannot remember right now, but not as a member of some Joint Command, but as the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps, who then reported to the Pristina Corps commander. I received information from those -- from those in attendance and also gave information at this one meeting or maybe two, but one I'm certain of that I attended. Also, I confirmed -- I confirmed that without being aware of any details that there were some documents of the Joint Command which were not signed, and I told you about this before you even asked me these questions. But I would like to assure you that for me, as the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps who had his superior in the corps commander, for me there was only the corps commander and no other commands. Even when the Chief of General Staff was in contact with me, I reported to the corps commander about what we spoke of. That's why I told you today that I'm not part of this story. I can agree in you in a way that looking formally at this when you pile up these documents, the conclusion can be drawn that some kind of command did exist, but this conclusion is not consistent enough."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: General, is it all right if we stop there? Does that cover the point you wanted to raise?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So, General, I think you've corrected me to suggest that in February and March of 2005 you told us that you may have attended two meetings of that body that I have called the Joint Command, instead of the five that we now know you attended from the meeting notes described in Exhibit P1468, correct?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. My intention and my request to Their Honours was directed towards the Prosecutor's allegation based on the previous video-clip, that I did not mention my presence at the meetings of the Joint Command at all, whereas I, even without being asked whether I had attended or not, when explaining what I knew about that group of people, about that body as it is called, about the coordination between the army and the MUP and various information, I explained that on one or two occasions I did attend this. That was the point of my request of Friday, not to challenge based on documents what the Prosecutor has introduced about my presence because it did occur on two occasions. There was one meeting in August and maybe three or four in September, but in my view these were two separate occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, General, we'll leave it to the Judges to review the record, but as I recall I was suggesting that you only mention attending only possibly one meeting in October regarding -- around the time that the OSCE came. But we'll let the Judges review the record. I want to ask you about that last statement you made on the tape. You say: "I'm not part of this story. I can agree in you in a way that looking formally at this, when you pile up these documents the conclusion can be drawn that some kind of command did exist, but this conclusion is not consistent enough." General, at that time when you were being interviewed, there were very few documents reflecting the existence of the Joint Command that Mr. Coo had and discussed with you. Since that time, as you know, there have been several additional documents, particularly some of those Joint Command orders in March and April 1999. How big does the pile have to get before we can change your mind and get you to agree that some kind of Joint Command did exist?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think there are other documents, except for the ones obtained by the OTP. Secondly, I can never accept the claim that there was some sort of Joint Command in command of the corps while I was the Chief of Staff and while I was the corps commander, never, I repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, General. Then let's go to your interview at page 47 of the English. You were talking about a report that the corps command made in -- around March the 5th, 1998. And I don't think we have a copy of this document, but you said that the corps questioned the army that the police in clashes with the terrorists used combat equipment which had the same colour as the equipment and devices the Yugoslav Army uses. And you say: "So we addressed this as a bad thing and that the army colours should not be used for such activities. To clarify, the police received this equipment from the army but not from the corps but from the General Staff, and they didn't paint -- but they did not paint them blue, which is the colour of the police." And if I can carry over to page 49 just to follow-up on to that. You said: "The problem was that some of these vehicles did not have MUP licence plates, which were blue, and they cannot carry out their task because they see a military vehicle without any kind of licence plates. It's a technical problem for the army traffic police ... It could lead to misinformation both among the public and local population and civilians and international community that the army was doing something which it was not engaged in at the time." So how big a problem was that in 1998 that the MUP was -- some of the MUP was using VJ vehicles and had not painted them blue?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March I was still in the corps command in Pristina, and I remember a document in which the corps command reported to the 3rd Army command that on the Pristina-Klina-Pec axis some vehicles had been observed, military vehicles, meaning that they had military characteristics and were of a military colour, but they had no licence plates, and they were moving in a column of police vehicles. We stated the date when this was observed and we asked the army command that this be solved at a higher level. So this was a specific event, specific information that I had, and we drew attention to this information. To what extent this was a general problem, I couldn't reply now with any precision to that. I think additional measures were taken to harmonize all this with what should be -- what should be done to mark each of the structures. I don't know to what extent this was done because I didn't see all those forces and structures, but I do remember this particular document and I spoke about this in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you tell us at page 50 that the police had combat means from the army, weapons, also freight and field vehicles. And you said: "Between one and a half and five tonnes then anti-aircraft devices such as the Praga." What other kinds of vehicles did the army have -- did the police have from the army besides Pragas, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that in that document we also mentioned all-terrain vehicles with six seats of the AR-55 type; also one-and-a-half tonne vehicles, TAM, T-A-M, T-10, we had occasion to see those photographs here as Prosecution evidence; Praga which was an anti-aircraft defence means. And I'm not sure exactly when and where infantry combat vehicles such as the BOV, or rather, armoured combat vehicle. I didn't see that all over Kosovo. There was also an issue of M-60 personnel carriers and those are the vehicles I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not clear on the last couple of sentences of that last answer. Did the police have any army BOV-3 vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not refer to BOV-3 but to BOV-1, that's an infantry armoured combat vehicle. The BOV-3 was an anti-aircraft system. I know about the Praga but I'm not sure about BOV-3. The BOV-1 is a military police vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did the MUP have any of those, BOV-1s?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, they did, but I can't be a hundred per cent certain. I'm almost sure. I don't know whether the state security had their own helicopters, MiG 24, or whether they belonged to the army. I don't want to speculate here now, but there are documents at the level of the General Staff and the Ministry of Defence; because it was the Ministry of Defence that was in charge of that job. The General Staff didn't have the right [as interpreted] to deal with this matter without the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But the police did have some helicopters, you just don't know whether they were their own or whether they belonged to the army; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see a MiG 24 combat helicopter. I had information that this was being used by units from the state security, but I really don't know whether they belonged to the army or whether the State Security Service had obtained some, had procured some for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what colour were those helicopters?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I think they were the original colours from the producers. These were Soviet-made helicopters. I can't really be precise in my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise for interrupting my colleague, Mr. Hannis, but I don't want us to lose this in the transcript. I think there's a big mistake page 80, line 21, I think the General said that this was a matter within the competence of the Ministry of Defence and that the General Staff did not have the right to deal with this matter, whereas the transcript reflects the opposite, that the General Staff did have the right to deal with this matter without the Ministry of Defence. The response was the opposite.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes: He said: "Did not have the right."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, General, did the MUP have any other army weapons such as mortars, like the 82- and the 120-millimetre mortars?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what weapons and equipment they had. If one says they had a military mortar, one might suggest that they received it from the army, but the police forces could procure weapons directly from the manufacturers. They did have mortars, but I don't know whether they were procured from the army through the Ministry of Defence or whether they were purchased from the manufacturers. But it's true that they did have mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're aware this issue of the MUP possessing certain kinds of equipment from the army was something that was an issue in connection with the OSCE, the KVM mission, right? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VLADIMIR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecutor, maybe the interpretation is not quite right, but what does this mean, that this has to do with the KVM mission? I didn't really understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, actually it will help me to have a reference to a VJ collegium meeting to ask that question, so if I could do that tomorrow I'd like to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall adjourn now until tomorrow and resume at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of November, 2007, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
